subject: swampTroll
pitch:
Category: Monster.
Subject: swamp troll with tusks, mohawk and bone fetishes.
Style: Blizzard/Warcraft.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a three.js module for a swamp troll character with tusks, mohawk, and bone fetishes, aiming for that chunky, bold Warcraft/Blizzard aesthetic with painted textures, while keeping within part and texture count limits.

I'm working out which exports and kits to pull in from the builder SDK, considering whether to use a glow effect for the troll's eyes to give them an amber or green swamp-fire look that fits the creature's menace.

Now I'm recalling the precise API signatures I'll need—how joints, chains, sweeps, lofts, parts, sticks, and sprouts are constructed and what options each accepts—so the generated model actually compiles against the real SDK.

Continuing through more paint and texture helpers, plus limits (1000 parts, 60k triangles, 160 joints, 64 flat colors) and coordinate conventions (+Y up, +Z forward, +X left). I'm thinking through the design for a swamp troll: lanky, hunched, ~2.5m tall, long arms, big hands, tusks, mohawk, pointed ears, bone necklace and charms, loincloth, moss and mud detailing.

Working out the color palette — teal-green skin, moss, mud brown, bone ivory, dark olive mohawk — and planning the skeleton structure, starting with hip root position and a hunched spine chain built from a curved path up through chest, neck, and head joints.

Now I'm sizing things overall: roughly 2.4-2.6m standing height with a forward-hunched head, figuring where shoulders, head center, and mohawk tip land. For the skull I'm weighing sphere parts with scale versus a lofted shape built from stations along a curved path for a more sculpted brow and jaw.

I'll use lofted stations attached to the head joint, with the skull wide at the back and narrowing into a long jaw, positioned slightly forward and down from the neck. I'm working out how to express the local forward/up/left offsets for placing head features relative to that joint.

I'm adding a separate jaw joint for the lower head with its own loft, plus curved sweeping tusks protruding upward from the jaw like a classic troll design. For the eyes, I'm using glowing yellow spheres with dark slit pupils set sunken under the brow.

Now I'm shaping the brow ridge as a swept bezier curve, and for the ears I'm extruding a pointed leaf-like outline sticking out sideways, bone-attached to the head. For the mohawk, I'm planning a series of overlapping spiky fin shapes running along the midline from brow to back of skull, varying their height for a jagged crest look.

Each fin sits in the sagittal plane with its outline oriented forward-up and thickness extruded sideways, shaped like a tilted leaf or spike pointing up and slightly back, sized progressively smaller toward the rear — plus a base sweep ridge along the crown to anchor the hair silhouette before painting stripe colors on the fins.

For positioning, I'll avoid floating geometry by casting rays downward from above the head to find the actual skull surface and attach each fin's base to that hit point, ensuring the mohawk sits flush against the scalp curve.

Now I'm thinking through bone fetishes — necklaces with bone pendants and skull charms, a belt studded with bone fragments and a pouch, maybe bone bracers — built using rings and small primitive shapes attached at anchor points around the body.

For the detail textures, I'm planning the glowing slit-pupil eye as an SVG decal applied to the head surface near the eye socket, then wrapping it with a glow effect since decals return parts that glow() can target.

For additional textures, I'm thinking war paint swirls on the cheeks as another transparent SVG decal, plus a loincloth rendered as a textured box or plane part with a rune-embroidered band pattern rather than a swept geometry, since textures only apply to parts and sticks.

For the troll's shoulders, I want hanging moss strands using card geometry with a ragged moss-strand SVG texture, giving it that swamp-creature look. I'm also considering carved bone sigils for a skull pendant, but weighing whether to use a decal on the pendant's surface versus simplifying to a flat plane with the rune pattern, since decal targeting on a spherical pendant part adds complexity — I'll likely settle on around five total textures: eye, war paint decal, moss strands, and a couple more simple options to keep things manageable.

Now I'm sketching out the paint logic for skin, planning a custom shader that blends teal-green base tones with noise-driven mottling, adds moss coloring on upward-facing surfaces, and darkens toward the feet to simulate mud staining.

Still writing paint shader...

For the remaining materials, I'm deciding on texture functions for each part: a layered olive/ochre grain for the mohawk suggesting hair streaks, a mottled bone-white pattern for the tusks and bone totem, and a striped rust/ochre texture for the hide loincloth.

Now I'm counting out the part budget — head, tusks, brows, ears, eyes with decals, mohawk ridge with fins and bones, torso, shoulders, arms with segmented fingers and claws, legs with clawed toes, belt with bone pendants and pouch, and a beaded necklace ring — tallying toward the 180-340 part limit.

Moss cards batch as a single part despite rendering hundreds, so that stays cheap, putting the total around 150-250 parts which fits comfortably. The code itself will need to be lengthy, maybe 900 lines, so I'm being careful to verify API signatures like limb's bends parameter before writing the leg joints so the knee bends forward correctly.

For arms I'm working out how chain naming works: a path with N points needs N names to get a tip joint, so a four-point shoulder-elbow-wrist-hand path needs four names to produce the hand tip, and I'm planning to use the limb helper similarly for the arm bend direction.

I'm placing shoulder and hand targets for a relaxed troll pose, checking that the arm segment lengths allow a natural bend, and reasoning that elbows should point backward when arms hang down, so I'll use a negative-Z bend direction for the elbow joint.

Now I'm working out hip and foot target positions, making sure leg segment lengths sum to slightly more than the hip-to-foot distance so the knees bend naturally forward, and setting the ankle target height low near the ground to anchor the foot geometry.

Overall body height comes together around 2.5 meters, matching typical Warcraft troll proportions. Now I'm setting up the spine as a chain of joints curving from the hips forward to the chest and shoulders, naming each segment (waist, chest, shoulders) so the hunched troll posture reads correctly through the torso.

For the body surface, I'm figuring out how to loft a mesh skin over the spine chain and hips joint together so the torso geometry follows the curved spine path properly, matching station positions along the catmull-rom spine curve.

Then I'm sketching out station widths and heights at various points along the spine to shape a big barrel chest, pot belly, and heavy shoulders, plus thinking through how to add pauldron-style shoulder detail and a thick neck sweep bound to the chest-to-head bone chain.

For the neck and head, I'm working out a joint chain running from the shoulders through a couple of neck points up to the head, deciding where exactly the head joint should sit and how to orient its aim direction so it points forward correctly.

Now I'm laying out the head profile stations centered around (0,2.3,0.4), moving from nape through crown, brow, muzzle, to snout tip with widths and heights shrinking toward the front, planning to loft through these centers with a catmull curve.

For the jaw, I'm planning a separate joint positioned slightly forward and below the head, with its own loft stations running from near the throat to the lower snout, keeping the top of the jaw loft aligned with the bottom of the head loft around y=2.2 so the two pieces mesh cleanly.

Now I'm sketching lower tusks as curved bezier sweeps rising from the lower lip outward and up, tapering to a point with an ivory color and flat-to-point caps, and considering whether to add smaller optional upper tusks from the head for extra detail. For the eyes, I'm thinking about placing them as glowing decals on the head's surface using spherical coordinates to position them within the brow hollow.

For positioning, I decide a front-facing ray cast is cleaner than spherical coordinates—shooting a ray from in front of the head toward it should hit the brow/eye region directly, and I can use the hit's surface normal as the decal's facing direction. I'm checking that the eye coordinates fall within the head loft's width at that height so the ray doesn't miss and return null.

Now I'm thinking through the ears: pointed, sticking out sideways with a slight backward sweep, drawn as an outline in the plane containing the sideways and up axes with thickness extending along the forward-back axis.

Positioning the ear base relative to the head using local coordinates, with the extrude axis flipped for the mirrored right ear so the same outline works on both sides.

I'm setting a small thickness for the ear with a slight bevel, using the skin paint color for the extrude. I'm considering whether to add a darker inner-ear lobe as a second smaller extrude, but may skip it for simplicity, and thinking about adding a small bone or gold ring as ear piercing jewelry to match the troll theme.

Now I'm working out the mohawk: sweeping a hair ridge along a curved path from the brow across the crown to the nape, tapering the radius and attaching it to the head bone, then planning to add fins on top by casting rays downward to find the mohawk's surface.

Still defining fin geometry...

Confirming the rod signature puts color right after radius, so I'll keep the bone pins minimal. For warpaint, I'm planning a decal using tribal chevron lines in ochre and black across the cheeks and brow, with a transparent-background WARPAINT texture.

Working out the ray geometry to position the cheek decal correctly, computing azimuth and elevation angles from the head center toward each cheek point, and figuring out how to handle a null hit result safely.

I'm also thinking through the mirror parameter for the decal, since the eye texture needs to flip depending on whether it's placed on the left or right side of the face relative to the viewer.

For the hanging moss, I'll use a strand-based texture and scatter moss cards across the torso surface, filtering for points high up with upward-facing normals, then orient each card frame upright with its own lean for a natural hanging look.

Still working out the hanging card orientation...

Cards bind to the torso bone frame, scattered across the surface with around 60 cards total to stay within the triangle budget. For the moss texture, I'm sketching an SVG with dark green strands and lighter highlights to suggest hanging growth.

Now I'm sketching the bone necklace: a ring of small bead frames placed around a neck line, each bead rendered as a tiny sphere part attached to the ring's item frame.

Tilting the ring axis slightly so the circle of beads sits naturally around the sloped neck, then I'm thinking about whether to call b.ring directly or just use the per-item callback since items get placed automatically. I also need to add a bone pendant hanging at the chest center — a skull-like sphere with a jaw piece, suspended from the necklace.

Working out the pendant's cord path and where exactly it should attach on the torso — tracing through the spine curve's station points to figure out the chest's front z-offset, and untangling how the loft's width/height axes map to the body's actual width and depth given the spine's upward tangent and default orientation frame.

Continuing the cord sweep down to the pendant top, then I'm working out the belt around the hips using a loop around the hip joint with an appropriate lift and direction.

Good, the loop hits the surface so it's safe. Now I'm sweeping a thin tube along that belt path to form the physical belt geometry, then planning to scatter hanging fetishes (bones, teeth, bottles) around it using a placement helper that distributes items evenly along the loop.

I need each hanging piece to dangle straight down from its attachment point rather than along the belt's tangent direction, so I'm working out whether to use a frame's local offset or a moved-point helper to get a properly downward-oriented bone, then connect it with a thin capsule shape.

For the bone pendant shape itself, I'm considering building it from a merged cylinder-and-sphere geometry to get a knobbed bone look, assuming BufferGeometryUtils' mergeGeometries is available for use.

Actually, I'll skip the merge and just compose bones from a capsule shaft plus small sphere knobs at each endpoint, since that avoids merge compatibility issues while still giving the right visual effect. The remaining question is which bone/joint these knob spheres should attach to when hanging off things like a belt, so they move rigidly with the right body part rather than snapping to the nearest unrelated joint.

I can pass an explicit bone option to the capsule helper so it overrides the nearest-joint default, and the signature supports color before options. Then I'm sketching the skull pendant and jaw pieces using sphere and box geometry with scale adjustments, and planning to apply the bone-fetish treatment across the mohawk pins, necklace, belt, pouch, bracers, and anklet, while considering sphere-based shoulder pads for the armor.

Now I'm adding heavy shoulder mass using two scaled spheres painted as skin, then building the arm using a chain with three joints (upper arm, forearm, hand) swept with a thickness function that tapers from a thick shoulder to a narrower wrist, going for that classic bulky troll forearm look.

For the hands I'm sculpting a chunky fist shape anchored at the hand bone's tip joint, then planning finger placement on the palm using local offsets relative to the hand's forward-and-down orientation, aiming for four clawed fingers plus a thumb in the troll style.

I'm also setting up claw spikes directed down and forward from each fingertip, and starting to lay out the leg limb chain with hip, knee, and ankle points for symmetry.

For the feet, I'm planning a flat bulbous pad shape extruded sideways from an outline in the forward-up plane, running from heel to toe with appropriate thickness for width — essentially sculpting the foot profile before extruding it into a 3D pad.

I'm positioning the foot's origin relative to the ankle joint, dropping down to sole height and aligning the outline so it spans correctly from heel to toe around the ankle point.

Now I'm adding small claw spikes angled forward-down at the toe tips, then setting up the sweep geometry for thighs and shins using the leg chain's bone joints to create the knee bulge. I'm also sketching how the pelvic torso loft connects to the hips, and starting to plan a hanging loincloth as a flat extruded piece in front of the hips.

For the loincloth, I'm defining a trapezoidal outline with fringe points that hangs down from the belt level, extruding it in the x-y plane facing outward in z, positioned slightly in front of the pelvis near the torso's front surface.

Since extrude doesn't support textures, I'm switching to a textured plane instead for the loincloth so I can apply a tribal woven cloth pattern, using transparent pixels at the bottom edge to create the fringe cutout effect rather than modeling fringe as separate geometry.

I'm also tallying texture usage across the figure — eye decal, warpaint, moss cards, cloth, and now considering a RUNE texture for carved bone sigils, possibly applied as a small plane layered just in front of the skull pendant to suggest an etched rune rather than a flat sticker. I'll likely cap it around five or six textures total and skip adding runes to the wrist bracers to keep things simple.

Thinking through the pendant itself, I'm weighing whether to add a sixth texture depicting a carved skull face with hollow black eye sockets, rendered as a decal projected onto the pendant's spherical surface using a ray cast from in front of the bone straight back to find the hit point on the front face, which would let the drawing wrap naturally onto the curved shape rather than floating as a flat plane.

For the glowing effects, I'm confirming the eye decals will glow using the glow kit since decals return Parts and glow wraps Parts, with the underlying material being MeshStandardMaterial to support emissive texturing — I'll stick to just the eyes glowing rather than adding moss spores or a lantern, keeping the magical feel focused.

Now I'm moving to the brow ridge geometry, sketching out a swept bezier curve between brow points positioned relative to the head using local coordinate offsets for left/right, up, and forward to shape the ridge above the eyes.

I'm reworking these positions relative to the head joint itself, calculating brow, eye, snout, and jaw coordinates by offsetting forward and up from the joint location, and noting that the jaw point lands oddly close to the head geometry so I'll need to adjust. I'm setting up a helper function to compute head-local positions consistently for the loft stations, since the head joint's slight downward tilt means I need precise local-direction math rather than raw world offsets.

Now I'm defining the head loft stations one by one — nape, crown back, crown, brow, cheek, muzzle, snout tip — each with width and height values to shape the troll-like heavy brow and cheekbones tapering to a narrower snout. I'm then working out the jaw joint position underneath the head and starting to lay out the jaw's own loft stations using the same local-offset approach.

I'm deciding the jaw bone should be parented to the head joint and aimed toward a chin point so it naturally points downward, and considering whether to pose it slightly open or leave the rest pose closed since the mouth is built from separate upper and lower jaw pieces so it can later animate opening. I'm also thinking about adding a darker sweep along the mouth line to suggest the interior gap between the jaws.

Now I'm planning the smaller details: a few spike teeth alongside the tusks, a bulbous nose/snout bump near the muzzle tip, dark eye socket rings with a brow ridge sweep above, and horizontally angled ears positioned near the nape that I'll mirror across the x-axis for left and right symmetry.

Defining ear geometry...

Then I'm thinking through adding a small torus ring piercing through the ear base, oriented so its face points outward along the X axis, using the gold/bone material. I also start sketching out the mohawk's sweep path along the top of the head, beginning with the crown point.

Still placing mohawk path points...

For the fin blades I'm setting z positions, heights, and a tapered outline leaning slightly back with a thin x-thickness, then checking that rays cast downward from above correctly hit the skull surface to anchor each fin base, embedding it slightly into the skin along the normal. Now I'm moving to the eyes, casting a ray from the front at z=3 toward -Z to find the first surface hit near x ±0.105, y 2.36 for decal placement.

For the warpaint I'm figuring out cheek marking positions, first considering an angular placement around a computed head center, then switching to side rays cast from far +X and -X toward the model to hit the cheeks at roughly y 2.26, z 0.56, with decals oriented sideways to face outward on each cheek.

I want the warpaint design as tribal zigzag chevrons in dark plum and ochre on transparent skin-revealing SVG decals, and I'm checking the ray path at z 0.56 clears the ear geometry near z 0.38. Eyes get larger decals sized for a troll-like look, and now I'm sketching the torso spine as a catmull curve from hips through chest to shoulders for the skeletal chain.

For the hierarchy, I'm settling on hips as root with role "spine," then waist, chest, shoulders as successive spine joints, with the neck forming its own chain parented off the spine tip and curving upward and outward to the head.

I'm checking that the shoulder joint sits inside the torso boundary rather than outside it, so I adjust its x-position inward and verify the arm chain reaches from shoulder to hand target with a reasonable bend. I work through the elbow bend direction and confirm the hand's fingertip clearance stays plausible relative to troll proportions.

I'm now setting up legs mirrored from the hips, defining thigh/shin/ankle chains with forward knee bends, and planning the arm chain names and roles similarly, plus sketching how fists might be represented as simple spheres attached to the hand bone.

For shoulder detailing, I'm considering adding mass spheres at the arm roots for heavier shoulders, plus bone fetish touches like spike clusters or capsule bundles radiating from the shoulder top, and bracer bands around the wrists to tie into the fetish/bone armor aesthetic.

Working through forearm band placement, I'm realizing the loop-cutting plane through the forearm joint will pass near the elbow rather than the wrist, since the joint position corresponds to the elbow end of that bone segment — so I'll need to adjust where the cut plane actually lands to get the bracer in the right spot.

Given the risk of chaining too many speculative API calls, I'm deciding to simplify: skip the loop-based bracer approach if it's too fragile and instead keep the sweep simple and well-documented. Moving on to plan the feet/toes and a belt pouch as a basic box shape.

Now I'm compiling the full bone-fetish decoration list for the troll — necklace beads, a skull pendant, hanging belt charms, a tooth pouch, mohawk bone pins, shoulder spikes, rune-plated bracers, and bone hoop earrings, while skipping an anklet or tail since trolls don't have one. I'm also considering scattering moss cards across the shoulders, head, and back, capped at 90 cards for performance.

For materials, I'm working out a countershading approach — a darker tone on the back blending into a paler belly — and sketching out a teal-green swamp troll skin palette as the base color.

Writing skin paint function...

Defining remaining paint textures...

For cards I'll pass white so the moss texture's own greens show through without tinting, and for the glowing eyes I'll keep the yellow-black coloring rather than greying it out. Now I'm sketching the SVG for the troll eye texture with a glowing iris and slit pupil...

Refining almond eye shape...

Still writing SVG eye code...

Now I'm designing a separate warpaint overlay with tribal chevron lines in dark brown and gold accents, including a small accent circle.

Writing moss strand SVG...

Now I'm working out the attachment logic: a card's bottom edge sits at its root on the frame, growing along the frame's facing axis, so a lean of 180 means the card grows downward from that root point rather than upward.

With moss, I'm confirming the wide base of each strand attaches at the shoulder and tapers to a tip at the top, sizing the moss card around [0.07, 0.34] with that 180 lean.

Now I'm sketching the loincloth shape for the cloth card -- a rectangular top band with a fringed, tasseled bottom edge, building it as an SVG path.

For the fill, I'm layering a brown base hide color with an ochre zigzag stitch band and a red accent band, plus a central rune circle, and sizing the plane geometry to roughly match the 64:70 aspect ratio of the drawing. Then I'm moving on to the bone rune sigils, planning dark carved stroke lines on a bone-colored background.

For bracer rune plates, I'm figuring out how to decal rune textures onto the forearm surface, using nearest-point lookups to position them correctly facing outward, and sketching how a sweep band around the wrist could carry two rune decals on its front face.

For decals more broadly, I'm reasoning through what object types accept decal targets—confirming that Sweeps (from loft) and Parts both work fine as surfaces—so I can apply eye decals onto a lofted head shape and skull decals onto a pendant part using ray casting to find the attachment point.

I'm sketching the skull SVG itself: a cranium outline, two eye sockets, a triangular nose cavity, and teeth lines, using ivory and dark brown tones to decorate the pendant sphere.

I'm also reconsidering the head loft's sweep resolution—with only 8 sides per cross-section it'll read as deliberately chunky and faceted, which fits the low-poly style I'm going for.

Next I want to add stylized exaggeration like oversized hands, plus shoulders, hips, and a rounded belly bulge using an extra scaled sphere part positioned along the spine.

For the torso loft, I'm working out stations along the spine path with widths and heights tapering from hips to waist to belly to chest to shoulders, using the catmull spine curve so the chest sits forward for a slight hunch. The spine chain is built from the same path so joints align, giving a smooth loft skin between the hip and spine bones.

Then I'm defining the neck as its own chain branching off the shoulders, with a tapering sweep radius narrowing toward the top, and checking that the chain's span count matches its joint names. The head joint attaches to the end of the neck chain, positioned just past where the neck sweep terminates so the loft transitions cleanly into the head.

For the jaw, I parent it to the head using local coordinates relative to the head frame, placing it slightly forward and down with an aim point further forward for the jaw's projection. Then for the eyes, I'm setting up ray casts against the head surface alone (not the full model) to place the eye decals, shooting rays from in front of the face toward the head loft surface.

For the mohawk fins, I'm casting rays from directly above to find the top intersection points on the head surface, since the geometry isn't being posed so I don't need to worry about re-querying after transforms.

Now I'm setting up a ring of beads for a necklace, generating frames around a circle positioned at the neck and using those frames to seat sphere and tooth-shaped bead geometries, alternating colors and shapes every few beads to vary the necklace's look.

I'm working out the neck's actual radius at the ring's height by interpolating between nearby profile points, then adjusting the ring's center and radius so the beads sit just outside the neck surface rather than intersecting it, and I'm positioning a skull pendant to hang against the chest by estimating the torso's front z-coordinate at that height.

I'm routing a cord from the neck ring down to the pendant using a curved path through a midpoint, checking that the midpoint doesn't poke into the chest geometry, then placing a decal on the pendant's front surface via a ray cast and sizing it to fit. Now I'm setting up a belt loop around the torso at hip height using a closed path with a slight lift offset.

I'm sweeping the belt as a tube along that path, then scattering charms along the front portion of the belt using a parametric range — working out which angle/t-value corresponds to the front since loops start their parameterization at the direction closest to world up, so I need to pick a from/to window that keeps the charms centered on the front face.

I'll just space 8 charms evenly around the whole belt, alternating bone, tooth, and pouch shapes hanging from short cords attached at each frame's local "down" direction — simpler than isolating just the front arc, and it reads fine since a troll would plausibly wear trinkets all the way around.

For helper functions like the bone fetish shape, I'll define them as closures inside the main build function so they can capture the builder instance `b` without needing to pass it as a parameter everywhere, keeping the types manageable. I'm also setting up the type imports from the SDK — PointInput, JointRef, ColorInput, Paint, Frame, Joint, DirectionInput, Fill — pulling in whatever the kit exposes for these shapes.

Still sorting out imports...

Finishing the import list, then setting up color constants and paint functions for skin tones using noise-based blotching for organic texture.

Adding more material definitions...

Cord color set, plus claw and mouth hex values defined. Now starting the build function with the troll's name, description, and a 2048 paint size before constructing the body piece by piece.

Deciding against larger paint resolution since 1024 gives sufficient texel density for the mottled skin texture across the troll's surface area. Starting to sketch a fetish helper function signature and the hip joint definition...

Still writing skeleton joints...

Defining arm limb points and chains...

For legs I'm mirroring the same pattern: computing hip-to-ankle limb points with thigh/shin/ankle joint names, parented to hips and grouped under "legs."

Now I'm moving to body mesh construction, lofting the torso through a series of station points along the spine path with width and height values that taper from hips to chest, using the spine bone pair for skinning. I'm also adding a belly paunch sphere positioned near the hips to give the torso some shape, scaling it to flatten slightly against the torso surface.

Next I'm defining the shoulder spheres attached to the upper arm joint, then setting up the arm sweeps with a radius function that tapers smoothly from shoulder to wrist, using a four-value evenly-keyed array for the upper arm and forearm sections.

I'm now adding the hand sphere positioned slightly down and forward from the arm's tip joint, giving it a flattened, elongated fist shape, and beginning to lay out the finger positions with spacing offsets for each digit including the thumb.

Still writing finger geometry...

Still placing thumb and finger joints... Now thinking through leg geometry -- sweeping a chain from hip through knee to ankle, tapering the radii from thick at the thigh down to narrower at the ankle for that troll-like leg shape.

Then I'm building the foot: an extruded outline positioned at the ankle joint, oriented so the sole sits flush with the ground and the foot is centered correctly on the leg's x-position.

I'm adding three claw-like spikes to the toes at the front of the foot, angled slightly downward and spread evenly across the width.

Checking that the toe tips don't dip below the ground plane, bumping the down offset for safety since the foot's lowest point should rest right at the floor, within acceptable sink tolerance.

Now I'm positioning a loincloth plane on the hips, oriented to face forward with its texture, and I'm working out the correct vertical center so its top edge lines up with the belt height.

I also want to make sure the cloth clears the thighs in depth and double-check that the belt sweep sits just in front of the torso, so the layering order between belt, cloth, and torso looks right at the front.

For the belt pouch, I'm placing a small box shape at the hip's front-left, keeping it simple rather than lathing a rounded shape.

For the mohawk, I'm sweeping a ridge crest along a catmull curve above the head with tapering radii, then starting to build out mohawk fins as a surface loft.

Now I'm raycasting down onto the head surface at several z-positions to find mounting points for each fin, extruding a small sharp-tipped triangular blade at each hit point along the head's curvature. I'm second-guessing whether the triangle outline's "sharp" corner tag will satisfy the OutlinePoint type when written as an inline array literal, weighing whether to import the type explicitly or just let it slide since it's a runtime script.

I decide the cleanest fix is to write a typed helper function that returns the tuple array with its literal type annotated inline, avoiding the readonly issues of `as const`. Beyond the fins, I'm now sketching a couple of small bone pins poking out from the crest of the mohawk as decorative knobs, figuring out reasonable height offsets so they sit just above the tallest fins without clipping through them.

Then I move on to the brow ridges, planning them as a swept bezier curve on each side of the head using mirrored left offsets, with control points positioned to hug the head loft surface slightly outward so they read as a raised ridge rather than floating detached.

For the eyes, I'm casting rays from in front of the head toward the surface to find the hit point, then placing a decal there sized to match the eye artwork's aspect ratio, mirroring it for the opposite side, and adding a glow effect to make it pop.

For the ears, I'm defining an extrusion that builds the ear shape outward from a point anchored just inside the head's surface, with a pointed tip marked as a sharp vertex and smoothing applied elsewhere. I'm sketching the ear outline as a series of coordinate points forming the characteristic ear curve, with a type definition to allow marking certain points as sharp corners.

Now I'm adding an inner ear shape too, positioning it slightly forward of the outer ear so it actually protrudes past the outer ear's surface instead of being hidden inside it, and giving it a slightly darker tone to suggest the inner lobe.

Next I'm working out ear-ring placement -- a small torus hung at the lower edge of the outer ear outline. I need to figure out the right orientation and axis so the ring reads as encircling the ear edge rather than floating oddly off to the side.

Then I'm moving to the lower tusks, positioning their base points near the mouth front relative to the jaw bone, using head-local coordinates to find where the tusk should emerge from the lip area.

Thinking through the curve: base around (2.2, .66), control point curving up and outward, tip rising above the lip with slight forward offset so the tusk arcs upward like a classic warcraft-style tusk shape. I worry the tusks might embed slightly into the head surface near the snout, but since they're curved sweeps, some overlap should be visually fine -- I'll nudge the forward offset a bit to reduce it.

Writing the tusk sweep code with a tapered radius down to a sharp point and rounded base cap, then starting on the smaller upper tusks near the upper lip.

For the mouth seam I'm sketching a dark catmull-rom curve running along the jawline where head meets jaw, giving it a subtle dip at the center to read as a mouth line, then adding a small flattened sphere for the nose with asymmetric scaling.

For the warpaint I'm casting rays from either side of the head inward to find the surface hit points, then placing decals there sized to fit the cheek area -- making sure the ray direction flips correctly for the left and right sides.

For the pendant, I'm adding a small flattened sphere bone attached to the chest joint, then raycasting onto its surface to place a skull decal, and considering whether to add a tiny jaw piece beneath it for extra detail.

Now I'm working on a cord sweeping from the base of the neck ring down to the top of the pendant using a curved spline, then building the necklace ring itself as a circular arrangement of beads around the neck, mixing in occasional tooth-shaped spikes every few beads, all parented under a "necklace" group.

For bead coloring, I'm alternating between bone and dark wood tones. Then I'm constructing the belt out of a loop traced around the torso surface, sweeping it with a hide-colored cross-section, and walking along it to hang alternating cord-and-charm drops -- cycling between bone sticks, fetish bone pieces, and tooth charms -- making sure these charms inherit the hip bone so they move naturally with the body.
